title: Why Your Family Never Pays You Back

beats.text: At Thanksgiving, Dave asks his brother for three thousand dollars back. Mom is watching. Danny says, “I thought that was a gift.”
Rewind to April. Danny's car died, so Dave sent his entire emergency fund. The contract? A pizza emoji. No due date. No plan.
Danny paid his car loan, phone bill, and credit card on time. Dave got nothing. Then Dave's tire blew, and he put four hundred dollars on a credit card.
Payday is a deli line. The landlord gets served first, then the car lender, phone company, and credit card. They can punish late payment. Dave can't. So he's last.
Bankrate's 2025 survey found that of people who lent money expecting repayment, forty-four percent lost money. Twenty-six percent said the relationship was damaged.
Danny may not be a villain. He may be broke. But without a written plan, Dave is the easiest person to postpone.
The IRS says you need evidence that money was a loan, not a gift. A written note and repayment schedule help. A pizza emoji doesn't.
Dave calls privately. One page: three thousand dollars, one hundred twenty-five monthly, the day after payday, for twenty-four months. Both sign. Danny automates the transfer.

Now Dave has a date in the line. Before lending again, he asks: “Is this a gift, or a loan?” If it's a loan, write down the terms. If losing it would hurt, say no—or give only what you can afford as a gift.
